k1p1-2.name: text#2
k1p1-2.text: KP03 The label decides: classification or regression

k1p1-28.name: text#28
k1p1-28.text: Similar inputs, different kinds of answer

k1p2-2.name: text#2
k1p2-2.text: Supervised learning: every input comes with a label

k1p2-31.name: text#31
k1p2-31.text:
A label need not be text:
it can be a category name or a measured value

k1p2-33.name: text#33
k1p2-33.text: With labels there is an “answer” to train on

k1p3-2.name: text#2
k1p3-2.text: Classification picks a class; regression, a number

k1p3-5.name: text#5
k1p3-5.text: Classification: one of finitely many classes

k1p3-33.name: text#33
k1p3-33.text:
on a continuous line,
any position is possible

k1p3-35.name: text#35
k1p3-35.text: Output type: a finite set of classes, or a real number?

k1p4-2.name: text#2
k1p4-2.text: Categories and diameters are not one scale

k1p4-36.name: text#36
k1p4-36.text: A class is a name; a diameter difference is meaningful in cm

k1p5-2.name: text#2
k1p5-2.text: A numeric label: identifier or measurement?

k1p5-23.name: text#23
k1p5-23.text: Both are numbers: identifiers don't support arithmetic, measurements do

k1p6-2.name: text#2
k1p6-2.text: One score: take its sign, or keep its size

k1p6-60.name: text#60
k1p6-60.text: scores of samples 1 to 12; the line is 0

k1p6-62.name: text#62
k1p6-62.text: Same 12 points, same parameters: only the output rule differs

k1p7-51.name: text#51
k1p7-51.text: $f_\theta^{\mathrm{cls}}(\mathbf x)=\begin{cases}\ell_2,&s(\mathbf x)\ge0\\\ell_1,&s(\mathbf x)<0\end{cases}\qquad f_\theta^{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbf x)=s(\mathbf x)$

k1p7-55.name: text#55
k1p7-55.text: These values cannot give accuracy or diameter error

k1p8-2.name: text#2
k1p8-2.text: Seeing a probability does not make it regression

k1p8-27.name: text#27
k1p8-27.text:
The task depends on
what is finally predicted

k1p8-28.name: text#28
k1p8-28.text: A probability of a binary event is a continuous value, yet it can be estimated from “did it happen” labels

k1p8-29.name: text#29
k1p8-29.text: State the target first, then how the output is used

k1p8-31.name: text#31
k1p8-31.text: Numbers inside do not fix the final output rule

k1p9-2.name: text#2
k1p9-2.text: What if we remove the labels and keep only inputs?

k1p9-60.name: text#60
k1p9-60.text: Next, KP04: with no answers, what structure is in the data? $\to$

steps.label: KP03 The label decides: classification or regression
The label decides the task · 1/9
steps.speakerNotes: Asking which fruit it is and asking its diameter can use similar inputs but need different answers. (The fruit is an analogy.)

steps.label: The label decides the task · 1/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The first question: choose one from a finite set of categories.

steps.label: The label decides the task · 1/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The second: answer a measured value, such as 7.2 cm.

steps.label: The label decides the task · 1/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The number of category names does not count the possible diameters. The label's meaning identifies the task.

steps.label: Inputs paired with labels · 2/9
steps.speakerNotes: Supervised learning uses paired inputs and targets. A target is also called a label.

steps.label: Inputs paired with labels · 2/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Each input x comes with a label y.

steps.label: Inputs paired with labels · 2/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A label need not be text: it can be a category name or a measured value.

steps.label: Inputs paired with labels · 2/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Labels give us answers to train on.

steps.label: Two output types · 3/9
steps.speakerNotes: Formally: classification maps an input to one of m classes; the regression here maps to one real number.

steps.label: Two output types · 3/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Classification: pick one of finitely many classes; here the second is picked as a sketch.

steps.label: Two output types · 3/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Regression: the output is a real number on a line, such as 7.2 cm.

steps.label: Two output types · 3/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: They can use the same input features and still be different tasks.

steps.label: Class vs diameter · 4/9
steps.speakerNotes: The note's example: 3 hypothetical teaching samples with the original numbers. Descriptions need encoding before they become vectors. Note: the source calls them 3 apples, but the second is labeled a cucumber.

steps.label: Class vs diameter · 4/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: On the right are the diameters: 7.2, 6.8 and 6.5 cm, bars to scale.

steps.label: Class vs diameter · 4/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Class 1 and class 2 are names, not a claim that one is twice the other. A diameter difference such as 7.2 minus 6.5 equals 0.7 cm is meaningful.

steps.label: Class vs diameter · 4/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Even when a label is written as a number, ask whether it is an identifier or a measurement.

steps.label: Identifier vs measurement · 5/9
steps.speakerNotes: A class identifier is just a name: class 2 is not twice class 1, so identifiers don't support arithmetic.

steps.label: Identifier vs measurement · 5/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: A measurement differs: 7.2 minus 6.5 equals 0.7 cm, and the difference carries units.

steps.label: Identifier vs measurement · 5/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: So when a label is a number, first ask whether it is an identifier or a measurement.

steps.label: Identifier vs measurement · 5/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: (The diameters are the note's hypothetical teaching samples, not real measurements.)

steps.label: One score · 6/9
steps.speakerNotes: Now the note's 12 unitless points. Reuse KP02's weighted sum with both weights 1 and offset b set to minus 5. Changing b from 0 to minus 5 only exposes both signs; it is not a training result.

steps.label: One score · 6/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Classification looks at the sign of the score: the boundary is x1 plus x2 equals 5. Non-negative scores go to class 2, negative to class 1.

steps.label: One score · 6/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Of the 12 points only the first has a negative score, minus 1.5, so it is class 1; the other 11 are non-negative. The two points on the boundary have score 0 and go to class 2.

steps.label: One score · 6/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Regression keeps the score itself: on the right are the 12 scores. These are not real fruit labels.

steps.label: Two output rules · 7/9
steps.speakerNotes: Sample 1 (1.5, 2.0): the score is 1.5 plus 2.0 minus 5, equal to minus 1.5. Classification outputs class 1, regression outputs minus 1.5. Sample 7 (8.0, 7.5): score 10.5, class 2, regression 10.5.

steps.label: Two output rules · 7/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Put the two scores on a line: 0 is the classification boundary, class 1 on the left and class 2 on the right.

steps.label: Two output rules · 7/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Two rules: classification picks class 2 for a non-negative score and class 1 for a negative one; regression outputs the score. These are not observed fruit labels or cm predictions, so they cannot establish accuracy or diameter error.

steps.label: Two output rules · 7/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: All values were computed by program.

steps.label: Probability and task · 8/9
steps.speakerNotes: Common misconception: seeing an internal value and concluding the task is regression. This page is a supplement. A classifier can compute class scores or probabilities, then choose a class. (0.8 is a sketch, not the note's number.)

steps.label: Probability and task · 8/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The input first yields an internal score or probability.

steps.label: Probability and task · 8/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Then a rule chooses the class. A binary-event probability is continuous yet can be estimated from categorical event labels, so the claim that rain probability must be regression is too strong.

steps.label: Probability and task · 8/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: State the target, then how the output is used. Binning diameters makes a different classification task with a different scoring rule and resolution. Classification and regression are common supervised tasks, not all of them.

steps.label: Remove the labels · 9/9
steps.speakerNotes: What the two tasks share is a target to train on.

steps.label: Remove the labels · 9/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: What if we remove the labels and keep only the inputs?

steps.label: Remove the labels · 9/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: There is no answer to compare against. The next unit asks what structure the data itself has.

steps.label: Remove the labels · 9/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The note's practice questions stay in the note.
